messages.author: b497afe6ddc8398c
messages.subject: Clarification on meta-analysis models
parts:
Hi everyone,

I have a question about the meta-analysis model in brms. These are models of the form
yi | se(sei) ~

It is my understanding we are using this to fit this mathematical model. Let yi be the effect sizes and sei be the standard errors of the effect size. 

Then we assume
yi ~ normal(theta_i, sei^2)

where theta_i is study's "actual" effect size. Then
theta_i ~ normal(mu, tau^2)

 And mu and sigma have priors, maybe something like
mu ~ normal(0, 10)
tau ~ cauchy(0, 3)

This mathematical model is described here, with Stan code: http://mc-stan.org/users/documentation/case-studies/divergences_and_bias.html

So here is a real example. You can find the data set in this github repo, but any data should work. 

m <- brm(effect_size | se(standard_error) ~ 1 + (1 | study), data = d)

But how do I sample the tau parameter of this model? 

If I call 
posterior_summary(m)
I don't see any parameter that looks like the tau in the mathematical model.

What am I missing? 

I've also tried 
se(standard_error, sigma = TRUE)
but I don't think that is what I want. For example, in the Stan code of the model with sigma true, I see
normal_lpdf(Y[n] | mu[n], sqrt(sigma^2 + se2[n]))
which doesn't seem like what I want. 

Maybe this what I'm looking for, but I'm not familiar with that parameterization. And if this is what I want, why is sigma=TRUE not the default (like it is in the Stan 8 schools model linked above)? It was briefly discussed here, https://github.com/paul-buerkner/brms/issues/114 but I'd be interested in the background. 

Thanks,

Tim

messages.author: b497afe6ddc8398c
messages.subject: Re: Clarification on meta-analysis models
parts:
Okay, I think I see what's going on. Sorry for the beginner question.

I believe brms by default uses the parameterization

y_i ~ normal(m + theta_i, sei)
theta_i ~ (0, tau)


and then we can include priors on the average 

m ~ normal(0, 10)

and on tau

tau ~ cauchy(0,3)


if we would like. 

Therefore, in the model tau is sd__study__Intercept.

Sorry for the trouble, maybe my confusion will help some one else.

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Re: Clarification on meta-analysis models
parts: Indeed, in
m <- brm(effect_size | se(standard_error) ~ 1 + (1 | study), data = d)

sd__study__Intercept is tau.

The reason sigma is set to FALSE by default in se has to reasons: First (and most importantly) it ensure backwards compatibility. Second, estimating tau via a random effect instead of directly via sigma is in line with how other packages handle it and also allows for better plotting of study effects. See for instance https://vuorre.netlify.com/post/2016/2016-09-29-bayesian-meta-analysis/

parts:
Thanks for the super fast answer. I'm still confused on how a model with one parameter less would give me the same answer, but yes, the three models give the same intercept:

I first simulated data similar to the 8 schools, but now there are 4000

J <- 4000
mu <- 4
tau <- 2
sigma <- runif(J,13,17)
theta <- rnorm(J, mu, tau)
y <- rnorm(J, theta, sigma)
schools_dat <- list(J=J,y=y,sigma=sigma)



And I fit it with non-centered parametrization model given as an example in http://mc-stan.org/users/documentation/case-studies/divergences_and_bias.html

fit_ncp80 <- stan(file='eight_schools_ncp.stan', data=schools_dat,
                  iter=2000, chains=4, control = list(adapt_delta = .99))
print(fit_ncp80, pars=c("mu", "tau"),probs=c(.0275,.975))

#     mean se_mean   sd 2.75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
# mu  3.78     0.0 0.24  3.31  4.24  4000 1.00
# tau 2.30     0.1 1.05  0.21  4.08   114 1.03



Then I tried with the two brms models

fit_brms<- brm(y | se(sigma) ~ 0 + intercept, data=data.frame(y= schools_dat$y, sigma = schools_dat$sigma),
    prior= c(prior(normal(0,5), class = b)
             )
    )
fit_brms
# Population-Level Effects:
#          Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat
# intercept     3.77      0.23     3.31     4.22       1581 1.00


I get more or less the same intercept.


fit_brms2<- brm(y | se(sigma, sigma= TRUE) ~ 0 + intercept, data=data.frame(y= schools_dat$y, sigma = schools_dat$sigma),
    prior= c(prior(normal(0,5), class = b),
             prior(cauchy(0,5), class = sigma)
             ), control = list(adapt_delta = .99)
    )

fit_brms2
# Population-Level Effects:
#           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat
# intercept     3.76      0.23     3.31     4.22       1274 1.00

# Family Specific Parameters:
#      Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat
# sigma     2.26      1.04     0.20     4.05        610 1.01

And here I also get the same intercept and more or less the same sigma (or tau in the Stan model).
The only difference is that the neff of the Stan model for the intercept is much higher, but then the neff of the sigma (or tau in the stan model) is higher for brms.

The slight differences in estimates and neff are possible also a result of different priors. The reason that this works is because in all three models the variance of a single observation yi is

var(yi) = sigma^2 + vi

where vi is the known sample variance supplied via se() in brms.

On Tuesday, January 30, 2018 at 9:24:02 AM UTC+1, Paul Buerkner wrote:
Indeed, in

m <- brm(effect_size | se(standard_error) ~ 1 + (1 | study), data = d)

sd__study__Intercept is tau.

The reason sigma is set to FALSE by default in se has to reasons: First (and most importantly) it ensure backwards compatibility. Second, estimating tau via a random effect instead of directly via sigma is in line with how other packages handle it and also allows for better plotting of study effects. See for instance https://vuorre.netlify.com/post/2016/2016-09-29-bayesian-meta-analysis/

I believe brms by default uses the parameterization

y_i ~ normal(m + theta_i, sei)
theta_i ~ (0, tau)


and then we can include priors on the average 

m ~ normal(0, 10)

and on tau

tau ~ cauchy(0,3)


if we would like. 

Therefore, in the model tau is sd__study__Intercept.
